title: Did the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act kill the R&D tax credit?
description: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) did not repeal or reduce the R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41.
summary: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) did not repeal or reduce the R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41. Its impact came from Section 174, which forced U.S. businesses to amortize research expenses over 5 years (15 for foreign research) from 2022 through 2024, until the One Big Beautiful Bill Act restored domestic expensing for 2025 onward.

body.text: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) did not repeal or reduce the R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41. Its impact came from Section 174, which forced U.S. businesses to amortize research expenses over 5 years (15 for foreign research) from 2022 through 2024, until the One Big Beautiful Bill Act restored domestic expensing for 2025 onward.
Law and guidance reflected: Internal Revenue Code as amended through Public Law 119-21 (July 4, 2025) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (released August 28, 2025).
Short answer

No. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97) did not repeal the research credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41. What it changed was the tax accounting treatment of the underlying research costs under IRC Section 174: for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, research and experimental (R&E) expenditures could no longer be deducted currently in the year paid or incurred and instead had to be capitalized and amortized ratably over 5 years (for domestic research) or 15 years (for foreign research). The Section 41 tax credit itself remained intact in the Internal Revenue Code, and its payroll tax offset election for qualified small businesses under Section 41(h) and Section 3111(f) was expanded by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-169) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022.

Subsequently, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025) added IRC Section 174A, which permanently restores a current deduction for domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, while foreign R&E expenditures remain subject to the mandatory 15-year amortization schedule under amended Section 174. The widespread perception that the TCJA "killed" the R&D tax incentive stems from the delayed Section 174 mandatory capitalization and amortization rules, which substantially increased current taxable income and cash tax liabilities for research-intensive businesses during the 2022 through 2024 taxable years, rather than from any repeal or reduction of the Section 41 credit itself.
What the TCJA changed, and what it left in place
The Section 41 credit was not repealed

The federal research tax credit was first enacted by the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (Pub. L. 97-34) on August 13, 1981, originally codified as IRC Section 44F. It was subsequently renumbered as Section 30 by the Deficit Reduction Act of 1984 (Pub. L. 98-369) and finally renumbered as Section 41 by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (Pub. L. 99-514), before being made a permanent fixture of the Internal Revenue Code by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-113). Section 13206 of the TCJA made a conforming amendment to Section 41(d)(1)(A) to align the definition of qualified research with the amended Section 174 rules, preserving the statutory link between the credit and Section 174 rather than eliminating the credit.

Moreover, the TCJA enacted corporate tax structural changes that indirectly increased the net value and usability of the Section 41 credit for many taxpayers. By reducing the maximum federal corporate income tax rate under Section 11(b) from 35 percent to 21 percent, the TCJA increased the net benefit of electing the reduced research credit under Section 280C(c) from 65 percent to 79 percent of the gross credit determined under Section 41(a). In addition, the TCJA repealed the corporate alternative minimum tax (AMT) under Section 55 and amended Section 38(c)(6) to treat corporations as having zero tentative minimum tax, removing a longstanding statutory barrier that had previously prevented many corporations from utilizing Section 41 credits against their regular tax liability.

Throughout the entire period, the research credit has continued to be computed either under the regular credit method, at 20 percent of qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year in excess of a statutory base amount (Section 41(a)(1)), or under the elective alternative simplified credit (ASC) method, at 14 percent of the QREs for the taxable year that exceed 50 percent of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years (Section 41(c)(4)(A), or 6 percent under Section 41(c)(4)(B) if the taxpayer had no QREs in any of the three preceding taxable years).
Section 174 moved from an elective deduction to mandatory amortization

IRC Section 174 was originally enacted on August 16, 1954 (ch. 736, 68A Stat. 66) as part of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. Before the TCJA amendment took effect for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, former Section 174(a)(1) permitted a taxpayer to elect to treat R&E expenditures paid or incurred in connection with its trade or business as current deductible expenses not chargeable to capital account, while former Section 174(b) offered an alternative election to treat deferred R&E expenditures as amortizable over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realized benefits from the expenditures (and taxpayers could also rely on Rev. Proc. 2000-50 to currently deduct or amortize software development costs).

TCJA Section 13206 rewrote Section 174 on a delayed effective date basis, applying to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Under the TCJA version of Section 174(a) and (b), "specified research or experimental expenditures" could no longer be deducted currently; instead, taxpayers were required to charge such expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a 5-year period, beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which they were paid or incurred, or over a 15-year period for expenditures attributable to foreign research (within the meaning of Section 41(d)(4)(F), meaning any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States). Because of the statutory midpoint convention, a calendar-year taxpayer could deduct only 10 percent (one-half of one-fifth) of a given year's domestic R&E expenditures in the first taxable year incurred, and only 3.33 percent (one-half of one-fifteenth) of foreign R&E expenditures in the first taxable year. Furthermore, TCJA Section 174(c)(3) explicitly mandated that any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software be treated as a specified R&E expenditure subject to mandatory capitalization and amortization, effectively superseding the current deduction option under Rev. Proc. 2000-50.

Hypothetical, for illustration only. Under the pre-2022 deduction election, the full $1,000,000 could have been deducted in 2022. (The 2025 and 2026 rows show the schedule as originally enacted; OBBBA transition elections discussed below can change it.)
Abandoned projects did not accelerate recovery

Under IRC Section 174(d) as amended by the TCJA, if any property with respect to which specified R&E expenditures were paid or incurred was disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the 5-year or 15-year amortization period, no deduction was allowed on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and the amortization deduction had to continue ratably over the remainder of the statutory 5-year or 15-year amortization period. Consequently, taxpayers could not write off unamortized R&E basis upon the failure or termination of a research project.
Accounting method change procedures

Under Section 13206(b) of the TCJA, the transition from deducting R&E expenditures to capitalizing and amortizing them was treated as a statutory change in method of accounting initiated by the taxpayer and made with the consent of the Secretary of the Treasury, applied on a cut-off basis for expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, with no IRC Section 481(a) adjustment allowed for prior taxable years. In Rev. Proc. 2023-11 (modifying Rev. Proc. 2022-14 and later incorporated into subsequent automatic change procedures including Rev. Proc. 2025-8), the IRS confirmed that while an accounting method change under IRC Section 446(e) and Treas. Reg. Section 1.446-1(e)(3)(i) generally requires filing Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method, under Designated Automatic Accounting Method Change Number 265), the requirement to file a formal Form 3115 was waived for the taxpayer's first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021. Instead, taxpayers were authorized to effect the automatic method change by attaching a short statement in lieu of Form 3115 to their timely filed original federal income tax return for that first taxable year, declaring the cut-off change and reporting the description and amount of specified R&E expenditures. Changes made in a taxable year subsequent to the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021 required a formal Form 3115 and a modified Section 481(a) adjustment taking into account only specified R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021.
Why it felt as though the credit had been killed

Analysis. This cash-tax timing shock follows mechanically from the 90 percent first-year deduction reduction shown in the 5-year midpoint amortization schedule above (and the 96.67 percent first-year reduction for foreign R&E).

The same analysis notes that companies which had never elected to claim the Section 41 research credit still had to identify, segregate, and track both direct and indirect research costs (including facilities, utilities, overhead, patent legal fees, and software development) in order to comply with Section 174. That is legally accurate because Section 174 is mandatory and non-elective, applying to all qualifying R&E expenditures paid or incurred in a trade or business regardless of whether a taxpayer claims a Section 41 tax credit, and because the scope of Section 174 R&E expenditures is substantially broader than the subset of direct costs (wages, supplies, computer rental, and 65 percent of contract research) that qualify as QREs under Section 41(b).
International interactions

items: Capitalization of R&E expenses at the controlled foreign corporation (CFC) level reduces current deductible expenses in computing tested income, which increases Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI) inclusions under IRC Section 951A on the U.S. parent's return (and may alter qualification for the GILTI high-tax exclusion election). Because most taxpayers account for GILTI as a period cost under Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) ASC 740, this increase in GILTI can directly raise the taxpayer's financial statement effective tax rate. Subpart F income under IRC Section 952 and Section 954 is affected in a similar manner.

Higher U.S. taxable income resulting from domestic R&E capitalization increases deduction-eligible income (DEI), which may proportionally increase the Foreign-Derived Intangible Income (FDII) deduction under IRC Section 250.
Higher regular taxable income increases regular tax liability relative to modified taxable income, making a Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT) liability under IRC Section 59A less likely.

R&E expenditures incurred by a foreign branch of a U.S. taxpayer are subject to the mandatory 15-year amortization schedule on the U.S. parent's tax return, increasing U.S. taxable income from the foreign branch operation without a corresponding increase in available foreign tax credits in the foreign branch basket under IRC Section 904(d).

The OBBBA restored domestic expensing

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) was enacted into law as Public Law 119-21, 139 Stat. 72, on July 4, 2025. Title VII, Section 70302 of the Act (139 Stat. 190-193) contains the statutory amendments governing domestic and foreign research and experimental expenditures.
Section 174A

New IRC Section 174A(a), added by Section 70302(a) of Pub. L. 119-21, permanently allows a current deduction, notwithstanding IRC Section 263, for any "domestic research or experimental expenditures" paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business. Under Section 174A(b), "domestic research or experimental expenditures" means research or experimental expenditures excluding any expenditures attributable to foreign research within the meaning of Section 41(d)(4)(F) (research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States). The provision applies to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Section 174A(d)(3) continues to provide that any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software shall be treated as a research or experimental expenditure, making domestic software development eligible for immediate expensing.

Alternatively, under IRC Section 174A(c), a taxpayer may elect to charge domestic R&E expenditures to capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures.
Foreign research stays on the 15-year schedule

IRC Section 174, as amended by Section 70302(b) of Pub. L. 119-21, is retitled and narrowed to apply exclusively to a taxpayer's "foreign research or experimental expenditures" (expenditures attributable to research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, or U.S. possessions under Section 41(d)(4)(F)), which must still be charged to capital account and amortized ratably over a 15-year period beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which such expenditures are paid or incurred. Furthermore, amended Section 174(d) provides that if any property with respect to which foreign R&E expenditures are paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the 15-year period, no deduction "or reduction to amount realized" shall be allowed on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and the 15-year amortization continues. Under Section 70302(e)(2) of Pub. L. 119-21, the added statutory prohibition against reducing the amount realized on disposition applies to property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025.
Transition: small business retroactive election

Under the statutory transition rule enacted in Section 70302(f)(1) of Pub. L. 119-21 (set out as an Effective Date and Transition note to 26 U.S.C. Section 174A), an eligible small business taxpayer that meets the gross receipts test of IRC Section 448(c) for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 may elect to apply the immediate domestic expensing rules of Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28, section 3.02(1), confirms that the inflation-adjusted Section 448(c) gross receipts threshold for a taxable year beginning in 2025 is $31,000,000, measured by the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts for the three prior taxable years (2022, 2023, and 2024).

Currency note. Section 70302(f)(1)(B) of Pub. L. 119-21 required the retroactive election to be made within one year of the July 4, 2025 date of enactment, and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 specifies that an election made by filing amended returns (or administrative adjustment requests under Section 6227 for BBA partnerships) for all affected taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 had to be filed on or before the earlier of July 6, 2026 (since July 4, 2026 fell on a Saturday) or the expiration of the statutory period of limitations for credit or refund under IRC Section 6511 (for example, April 15, 2026 for a calendar-year 2022 corporate return originally filed on April 15, 2023 without extension).
Transition: recovery of unamortized TCJA amounts

Under Section 70302(f)(2) of Pub. L. 119-21 (set out as a statutory note to 26 U.S.C. Section 174A), any taxpayer that capitalized and amortized domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 and before January 1, 2025 under the TCJA version of Section 174 may elect to deduct the remaining unamortized balance of those domestic expenditures either: (1) in full in the taxpayer's first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or (2) ratably over the two-taxable-year period beginning with the taxpayer's first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (or, if no election is made, continue amortizing the remaining balance over the original 5-year TCJA schedule). For a calendar-year taxpayer, this transition rule permits deducting 100 percent of unamortized 2022-2024 domestic R&E balances in 2025, or deducting 50 percent in 2025 and 50 percent in 2026.
Hypothetical example: unamortized balances entering 2025

Hypothetical. Assumes a calendar-year taxpayer that did not make the small business retroactive election and used the TCJA 5-year midpoint schedule. Domestic R&E paid in 2025 would be deductible under Section 174A(a) in addition, unless the taxpayer elects Section 174A(c).
Rev. Proc. 2025-28 accounting methods

IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28 was released on August 28, 2025 to provide procedural guidance for implementing the Section 70302 amendments of Pub. L. 119-21 under IRC Sections 174, 174A, 280C, and 446. Section 7.02 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 provides the automatic accounting method change procedures to transition to a Section 174A method and formally designates the following method names: the "§ 174A(a) deduction method," the "§ 174A(c) amortization method," the "small business retroactive method," and the "recovery of unamortized amount method." For an automatic change made under section 7.02 for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, the requirement under Treas. Reg. Section 1.446-1(e)(3)(i) to file a formal Form 3115 is waived, and attaching a compliant statement in lieu of Form 3115 to the tax return is authorized. Section 6 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 sets out the procedures for electing the Section 174A(c) amortization method (over not less than 60 months beginning with the month benefits are first realized) by attaching an election statement to the taxpayer's timely filed original return for the first taxable year to which the election applies.
Section 280C(c) coordination returns to the pre-TCJA pattern

During the 2022 through 2024 taxable years, the TCJA version of IRC Section 280C(c)(1) provided that a taxpayer's capitalized Section 174 basis was reduced only to the extent that the Section 41(a) research credit exceeded the allowable Section 174 amortization deduction for that taxable year—meaning most taxpayers neither suffered a reduction in their current amortization deduction nor needed to elect a reduced credit under Section 280C(c)(2) unless they wished to preserve full capital account basis for future years.

As amended by Section 70302 of Pub. L. 119-21 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, IRC Section 280C(c)(1) restores the traditional pre-2022 coordination rule to prevent a double tax benefit: the amount of any domestic R&E expenditures (as defined in Section 174A(b)) otherwise allowable as a deduction under Section 174A(a) or charged to capital account under Section 174A(c) must be reduced by 100 percent of the amount of the research credit determined under Section 41(a). Alternatively, under IRC Section 280C(c)(2), a taxpayer may avoid reducing its Section 174A deduction or capital account by electing on a timely filed original return (including extensions) to claim a reduced Section 41 research credit, equal to the gross Section 41(a) credit minus the product of that credit and the maximum corporate tax rate under Section 11(b) (currently 21 percent, yielding a net credit equal to 79 percent of the gross credit); once made for a taxable year, this election is irrevocable. For eligible small business taxpayers applying Section 174A retroactively to 2022-2024, sections 4 and 5 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 also provided special transition procedures to make a late Section 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election, or revoke a previously made election, for those retroactive years, subject to the same July 6, 2026 deadline.

In addition, Pub. L. 119-21 amended IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) so that to constitute "qualified research" for purposes of the Section 41 credit in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, the research expenditures must be eligible to be treated as domestic R&E expenditures under Section 174A, maintaining the strict statutory linkage between the credit and the underlying R&E expense provision.

body.text: The payroll tax election for qualified small businesses

Because the general business credit under IRC Section 38 and Section 41 offsets federal income tax liability, it historically provided limited immediate cash benefit to early-stage or pre-profit startups operating in a net operating loss (NOL) position with zero income tax liability. To address this, the PATH Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-113, Section 121(c)) enacted IRC Section 41(h) and IRC Section 3111(f) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2015, allowing a "qualified small business" (QSB) to elect to apply a portion of its Section 41 research credit against federal employer payroll tax liabilities. This payroll tax offset election remained fully in force throughout the TCJA period and was doubled in size during that period.
Qualified small business definition

Under IRC Section 41(h)(3)(A), a corporation (including an S corporation) or partnership (or an individual carrying on an active trade or business) qualifies as a QSB with respect to any taxable year only if it meets two cumulative statutory tests: (i) the gross receipts of such entity for the taxable year are less than $5,000,000, and (ii) such entity did not have gross receipts (as determined under the rules of Section 448(c)(3), including small amounts of interest or investment income) for any taxable year preceding the 5-taxable-year period ending with such taxable year. Furthermore, under Section 41(h)(4)(B)(ii), a taxpayer cannot make the payroll tax election for any taxable year if the taxpayer has already made such an election for 5 or more preceding taxable years, and under Section 41(h)(3)(B), an organization exempt from income tax under Section 501 is ineligible to make the election.
The Inflation Reduction Act increase

Under IRC Section 41(h)(4)(B)(i), the original annual payroll tax credit election limit enacted by the PATH Act was $250,000 per taxable year. Section 13902 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-169, enacted August 16, 2022) amended Section 41(h)(4)(B)(i) and Section 3111(f) to increase the annual limitation by an additional $250,000 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, raising the maximum annual payroll tax offset election to $500,000. Across the maximum five taxable years permitted under Section 41(h)(4)(B)(ii), five consecutive elections at $500,000 each total $2,500,000 ($500,000 x 5), compared with $1,250,000 ($250,000 x 5) under the pre-2023 limit; a QSB can reach that $2,500,000 cumulative maximum only if all five of its elected taxable years begin after December 31, 2022.
How the elected amount is applied

Under IRC Section 3111(f)(1) and (2), as amended by Section 13902 of Pub. L. 117-169, the elected payroll tax credit follows a mandatory two-tier statutory ordering rule for any calendar quarter: the credit is applied first against the employer's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (social security / OASDI) tax liability imposed by Section 3111(a) (6.2 percent of wages up to the social security wage base), up to the first $250,000 limitation, and any remaining elected credit (up to the additional $250,000 allowed under the IRA expansion, or any portion of the first $250,000 that exceeds the quarter's employer social security tax liability) is then applied against the employer's Hospital Insurance (Medicare) tax liability imposed by Section 3111(b) (1.45 percent of all covered wages). IRS guidance and Form 8974 instructions enforce this exact statutory ordering.

The Internal Revenue Code does not permit that. The statutory carryover in IRC Section 3111(f)(3) applies strictly after a valid annual election (capped at $500,000) has been made on Form 6765: if the elected payroll tax credit allocated to a calendar quarter on Form 8974 exceeds the employer's combined Section 3111(a) social security and Section 3111(b) Medicare tax liability for that specific calendar quarter, the unused portion of the elected payroll credit carries forward to the immediately succeeding calendar quarter to offset employer payroll taxes. By contrast, any Section 41 research credit generated in excess of the $500,000 annual election cap on Form 6765 is never converted into a payroll tax credit; it remains a regular general business income tax credit subject to the general 1-year carryback and 20-year carryforward rules under IRC Section 39(a)(1).
Forms and timing

To make the payroll tax offset election, the QSB must compute its research credit and designate the elected payroll offset amount in Section D of IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities), which must be attached to the taxpayer's timely filed original federal income tax return (including extensions) pursuant to IRC Section 41(h)(4)(A); the payroll election cannot be made on an amended income tax return. The elected amount from Form 6765 (line 44) is then carried over and reported on IRS Form 8974 (Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit for Increasing Research Activities), which is attached to the employer's quarterly federal employment tax return (such as Form 941, Employer's QUARTERLY Federal Tax Return, or annual Form 943 / Form 944 where applicable). Under IRC Section 3111(f)(1) and (2), the payroll tax credit is first allowed against employer payroll taxes in the first calendar quarter that begins after the date on which the QSB files its federal income tax return containing the Form 6765 election.
Controlled groups

Under IRC Section 41(h)(5)(A), all persons or entities treated as a single taxpayer under the aggregation rules of Section 41(f)(1)—including all members of the same controlled group of corporations (applying a more-than-50-percent common ownership threshold) and all trades or businesses (whether or not incorporated) under common control—are treated as a single taxpayer for purposes of the QSB payroll tax election. Consequently, the $5,000,000 gross receipts cap, the 5-year gross receipts history test, and the $500,000 annual election limitation apply on an aggregated basis to the entire controlled group as a whole, and any elected credit is allocated among group members in proportion to their respective QREs.

Qualified research still has to meet the statutory test

Under all three statutory eras analyzed in this report (pre-TCJA, the 2022-2024 TCJA amortization period, and the post-2024 OBBBA regime), the research tax credit is available exclusively for activities and expenditures that satisfy the four-part statutory definition of "qualified research" set forth in IRC Section 41(d)(1) (applied separately to each "business component" under Section 41(d)(2)(A) and the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(b)(2), and not falling within the statutory exclusions of Section 41(d)(4) such as post-commercial-production research, adaptation of an existing business component, duplication of an existing business component, surveys or routine quality control testing, foreign research, or funded research):

items: Section 174A / Section 174 Eligibility Test (Section 41(d)(1)(A)): The expenditures must be eligible to be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174A (for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, or under Section 174 for prior taxable years), meaning costs incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business which represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense aimed at eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process (Treas. Reg. Section 1.174-2(a)).

Technological in Nature Test (Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature, meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(a)(4)).

Permitted Purpose / Business Component Test (Section 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)): The application of that technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (defined in Section 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer), relating to a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality (Section 41(d)(3)(A)).

Process of Experimentation Test (Section 41(d)(1)(C)): Substantially all (at least 80 percent under Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(a)(6)) of the activities of the research must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose—requiring a systematic process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities (Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(a)(5)).

body.text: Furthermore, to withstand IRS examination and satisfy the general recordkeeping requirements of IRC Section 6001 and Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(d), as well as the heightened specificity requirements for refund claims on amended returns (first articulated in IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F and updated Form 6765 Section G business component reporting instructions), taxpayers must maintain contemporaneous technical and financial documentation substantiating the nexus between qualified employee wages, supplies, and contract research expenses and specific qualified business components.
Conclusion

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did not kill the federal R&D tax credit. IRC Section 41 remained in the Internal Revenue Code throughout, retaining its 20 percent regular credit rate and 14 percent alternative simplified credit rate, while the corporate rate reduction to 21 percent, the repeal of the corporate AMT, and the Inflation Reduction Act's doubling of the qualified small business payroll tax election to $500,000 (for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022) expanded the credit's accessibility. What the TCJA removed was the immediate current deduction for research and experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, replacing it with mandatory 5-year domestic and 15-year foreign amortization that inflated current taxable income for research-heavy businesses and diminished the combined near-term cash-flow benefit of R&D tax incentives from 2022 through 2024. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025) permanently restored immediate current expensing for domestic R&E expenditures through new IRC Section 174A for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, retained mandatory 15-year amortization for foreign research under amended Section 174, provided 1-year or 2-year transition recovery elections for unamortized 2022-2024 domestic R&E balances, and returned Section 280C(c) to its pre-TCJA coordination rules. Finally, the OBBBA's small business retroactive election permitting eligible taxpayers (with average annual gross receipts of $31,000,000 or less) to amend 2022-2024 returns was subject to a statutory deadline of July 6, 2026 under Rev. Proc. 2025-28, which has now passed.
